questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The members of a triad
questions.learningObjective: identify the root, third and fifth of a triad and say which note generates the others
questions.explanation: A triad has three members: a root, a third above it and a fifth above it. From C4 the third is E4 and the fifth is G4, so C4, E4 and G4 are the C major triad. B4 would be the seventh above C4, and adding it makes a seventh chord, not a triad, so the stack of four is one note too many. The reading cannot start on E4 either, because a triad built on E4 would need G4 and B4, and E4, G4, B4 is an E minor triad, a different chord built on a different root. The root is the note that generates the other two, which is why it can be found at the bottom of a close stack and then move elsewhere when the chord is inverted.
questions.hint: Ask which note generates the other two by stacking thirds above it.

options.text: Three of them, since C4, E4 and G4 are the root, third and fifth of a C major triad
Three of them, since E4, G4 and B4 are the root, third and fifth of an E minor triad
options.misconception: reads the stack from the middle note, so the chord is named on the third instead of the root

options.text: Four of them, since a seventh chord is also a stack of thirds built on the same root
options.misconception: treats a stack of four thirds as a triad, confusing a seventh chord with a triad

options.text: Two of them, since only the root and the third count as members of a triad at all
options.misconception: believes a triad has only a root and a third, forgetting that it also has a fifth

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The interval from a first-inversion bass to the root
questions.learningObjective: count the semitones from an inverted bass note up to the root of its chord
questions.explanation: Walking up the chromatic table from E3 gives E, F, F sharp, G, G sharp, A, B flat, B and C, which is nine note names and eight semitone steps, so the answer is 8. The second route is the octave: an octave holds 12 semitones and C4 lies a major third above C3, and E3 lies a major third above C3 as well, so the distance from E3 to C4 is 12 minus 4, which is 8. The letter count agrees, since E, F, G, A, B and C is six names and a sixth above the bass is exactly what a first inversion puts there. The trap is to answer 4, the interval from C up to E, which is the size of the chord's own major third and not the distance from the bass.
questions.hint: Count one semitone at a time upward from the bass, and check the letter count as well.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Testing a root against a function table
questions.learningObjective: trace a pitch-class lookup that flags a root outside the diatonic collection
questions.explanation: The pitch class of F sharp is 6 and the pitch class of C is 0, so the offset is 6 minus 0, which is 6, and 6 is not a key on the table. The rule therefore returns chromatic, which is the correct and useful answer: no diatonic chord of C major is built on F sharp, because a diatonic triad on the sixth degree is A minor and the note a semitone above it is foreign to the collection. In practice that label is the signal to look for a secondary dominant, since F sharp usually turns up as the third of a D major triad tonicizing the dominant. The wrong readings all force the value onto a key that exists in the table, which is precisely what the table was built to prevent.
questions.hint: Subtract the pitch classes, reduce mod 12, and then look the result up in the table.

options.text: chromatic, because 6 semitones above the tonic is not one of the seven diatonic positions

options.misconception: forces the offset onto a key that exists in the table, which is the error the table prevents

options.text: dominant, because a root a tritone above the tonic always carries dominant function
options.misconception: believes a tritone above the tonic is automatically the dominant of the key

options.text: predominant, because the rule maps every offset below seven onto the pre-dominant
options.misconception: misreads the table, which assigns pre-dominant function only to offsets 2 and 5

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Locating the pivot chord in a modulation
questions.learningObjective: identify the one chord in a progression that belongs to both of two keys
questions.explanation: A pivot chord is one chord that can be read in two keys at once, and the test is membership of two collections. D major contains F sharp, which is not in C major, so it cannot be any chord of C major, and D, F sharp and A are the second, fourth and sixth degrees of G major, which makes it the supertonic triad of G. That satisfies both halves of the definition. The G7 that follows is the dominant seventh of G, so it confirms the new key rather than enabling the change, and the D minor that precedes it is plainly diatonic to C. Reading the pivot as G7 is the tempting error because that is where the new key becomes audible, but a pivot has to be ambiguous at the moment it sounds.
questions.hint: Test each chord for membership in the C major collection, then read it as a chord of G major.

options.text: The D major chord, since D, F sharp and A form the supertonic of G major but no chord of C major
The G7 chord, since it is the only chord in the list that is built from four different notes
options.misconception: picks the chord that confirms the new key, which is by definition too late to be a pivot

options.text: The D minor chord, since a supertonic triad is the usual pivot in any modulation to the dominant
options.misconception: assumes the pivot rather than testing it, and picks a chord that is diatonic to both keys

options.text: There is no pivot here, since a modulation must begin on the tonic triad of the new key
options.misconception: believes a modulation has to start on the new tonic, when a pivot is a chord of both keys

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Root position against first inversion
questions.learningObjective: decide which of two voicings of one chord is in root position
questions.explanation: Both voicings contain exactly the notes C, E and G, so both are the C major triad and neither has gained or lost a member. What differs is the bass: the first has the root C lowest and is in root position, written I, while the second has the third E lowest and is in first inversion, written I with a six. Inversion is defined entirely by bass membership, so any arrangement of the upper three voices is possible above either bass note. This is why a chord can keep its identity while its figured bass number changes, and it is the reason the bass line, not the shape of the stack, is what a reader tracks when following a progression.
questions.hint: Compare the lowest note of each voicing against the three members of the chord.

options.text: Only the bass note, since a chord's inversion is decided by which of its members is lowest
The number of voices, since putting a chord in inversion adds a note to the chord itself
options.misconception: believes inversion adds a voice, as though the chord gained a new member

options.text: The kind of chord, since the second voicing is a seventh chord rather than a triad
options.misconception: counts four notes as a seventh chord, ignoring that one is a doubling of the root

options.text: The width of the upper voices, since inversion is fixed by the widest interval present
options.misconception: believes the widest interval decides inversion rather than the note in the bass

questions.topic: The span from a seventh chord's root to its seventh

questions.topic: Counting the tones a change of key holds in common
questions.learningObjective: trace a set-intersection rule that counts the notes shared by two chords
questions.explanation: The pitch classes of the first set are 0, 4 and 7 and those of the second are 0, 3 and 7, so the intersection holds 0 and 7, that is C and G, and the rule returns 2. Only two of the three tones survive, so this change of mode cannot be carried by a common-tone triad, because a common-tone modulation works precisely when the pivot shares most of its notes with the chord on either side. The reading of 3 is the tempting one, because a parallel triad looks like the same chord with a flattened middle, and only the count reveals that the middle is not shared.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Borrowed chords in a major key
questions.learningObjective: decide which chords in a passage lie outside the diatonic collection of the key
questions.explanation: The seven diatonic triads of C major are C major, D minor, E minor, F major, G major, A minor and B diminished, so four of the six listed are diatonic. F minor needs A flat, which is not in the collection, and A major needs C sharp, which is not either, so those two are borrowed. The minor subdominant is by far the commonest borrowing, because it makes a plagal motion sound unsettled and it is idiomatic wherever a passage is coloured by the parallel minor, usually for a phrase that ends in a half cadence. The reading that names D minor is a common slip, since a minor chord on the second degree is as diatonic as any other, and the claim that nothing is borrowed confuses a scale with the set of triads a style allows.
questions.hint: List the seven diatonic triads of C major first, then compare the passage against that list.

questions.topic: The four positions of a seventh chord
questions.learningObjective: name the inversion of a seventh chord from the note in its bass
questions.explanation: The chord has four members, the root G, the third B, the fifth D and the seventh F, and the position is fixed by which of them is lowest. Root position has G in the bass, first inversion has B, second has D and third has F, so the answer is F. That last position is the one with the seventh in the bass, and it is written with the figures four two because the intervals above the bass are a fourth to B, a sixth to D and an octave to G. It sounds the least stable of the four, since the note that wants to fall a step is the one on the bottom, and it is the position that gives a dominant seventh its urgency when it resolves.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Telling a chord tone from a non-chord tone
questions.learningObjective: explain the test that identifies a non-chord tone and name the kind it is
questions.explanation: Chord membership decides the question, and the reason is that a non-chord tone is defined negatively, as a note that is not in the harmony it sounds against. Duration, accent and loudness are all irrelevant to that definition, which is why a long accented dissonance can still be a passing tone and a soft repeated chord tone can still be a chord tone. Once the note is identified, its type is read off its neighbours, and here the D4 sits a step below the E4 and a step above the C4, both chord tones of the same triad, so it is a passing tone. The two traps are to test for dissonance, which would wrongly convict a passing tone of being an error, and to test for accent, which would wrongly promote a weak chord tone to the status of a melody note.
questions.hint: Ask which notes the held triad contains, then look at the neighbours of whatever is left over.

answer.exemplar: The test is membership, not emphasis or length. Hold the accompanying chord still and ask which of its tones each melody note contains: the C major triad is C, E and G, so the E4 and the C4 are members and the D4 is not. A note that is not a member of the chord sounding beneath it is a non-chord tone, however long it is held and however loudly it is sung. Having identified the D4, its type follows from its neighbours: it lies a step above the C4 and a step below the E4, it fills the gap between two chord tones of the same chord, and it is left by step in the same direction it was approached, which is the definition of a passing tone. The wrong belief to avoid is that dissonance is the test, so that any note creating a strong interval is called an error, or the reverse, that a melody note only counts as belonging to the chord when it sounds with the rest of the chord.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Tendency tones of a dominant seventh
questions.learningObjective: identify the two notes of a dominant seventh that are obliged to resolve
questions.explanation: The dominant seventh contains a tritone between its third, B, and its seventh, F, and a tritone of 6 semitones is the least stable interval available in tonal music. Its standard resolution moves each note by step in opposite directions, so B rises a semitone to C and F falls a semitone to E, and both of those notes are members of the tonic triad. The root G and the fifth D are free to go anywhere a voice can conveniently reach, which is exactly why the two chords of a cadence can be spelled in several voicings. The reading that moves the fifth upwards misunderstands the tritone, which resolves inwards, and the reading that sends the root down to E confuses the root's freedom with the tendency tones' necessity.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Why the dominant to tonic progression is the strongest
questions.learningObjective: explain what gives a dominant to tonic progression its strength in a key
questions.explanation: The dominant seventh contains a tritone between B and F, and the tonic triad contains no tritone, so the move from one to the other is the only place in the diatonic set where that unstable interval is obliged to collapse. B rises to C and F falls to E, both members of the tonic, and the bass lands on the tonic note, so nothing in the texture resists the arrival. That is what the word authentic means here: the progression is a resolution, not merely a change of chord. The three wrong readings each pick a feature that is not what makes the progression strong, since a fourth in the bass is a usual way to reach the tonic but not a guarantee, and the number of voices and of chord members affects weight rather than function.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Chords that share tonic function
questions.learningObjective: group chords by harmonic function and give the test that confirms the grouping
questions.explanation: Function groups chords by what they do in a progression, and the first, third and sixth degrees of a major key are grouped together because each is built from notes of the tonic triad itself. questions.learningObjective: explain the preparation, dissonance and resolution that make a suspension
questions.explanation: A suspension is defined by three stages, and all three are present here. The C4 is prepared, because it belonged to the harmony that preceded the change of bass and was consonant there. It is suspended, because once the bass reaches G2 the new chord is G, B and D and the held C is no longer one of its notes, so the voice has not moved while the harmony has. It resolves, because the C falls a step to B3 on the beat, arriving at a note of the new chord. The delay between the change of bass and the resolution is what the ear experiences as tension, and the interval figures record the motion, here a fourth above the bass falling to a third. The wrong belief is that the dissonance is an error, or that the note could be left hanging, when a suspension that never resolves is a fault rather than a licence.

answer.exemplar: Three things make it a suspension. First, the held C4 was a note of the previous harmony, so it was consonant when it was struck, and a suspension can only be prepared by a note that already belongs to the music. Second, the bass has moved to G2, which makes the new harmony G, B and D, and the held C4 is not one of those notes, so it has become a dissonance without any change in the voice that holds it. That contrast between a consonant beginning and a dissonant continuation is the whole definition, and it is why the figure is written as a held note tied across the barline rather than as a fresh attack. Third, the dissonance resolves by falling a step to B3, a note of the new chord, on the beat rather than before it, so the ear hears the friction released rather than avoided. The figures are named for the intervals above the bass, so a suspension that moves from a fourth to a third above its bass is written four three. The wrong belief to avoid is that the dissonance is a mistake to be corrected, or that the resolution may be delayed indefinitely: an unresolved suspension is a fault, and the downward step is what the ear is waiting for.

questions.topic: What makes a cadence perfect authentic
questions.learningObjective: explain the three conditions of a perfect authentic cadence and the role of each
questions.explanation: Perfect authentic is a compound term and each half of it is doing work. Authentic names the progression, dominant to tonic, which is what makes the pair a resolution at all. Perfect adds the two remaining conditions: the tonic chord must be in root position, so the bass sounds the tonic note and not the third or the fifth above it, and the tonic note must be in the highest voice, so that the line the ear is following arrives on the goal. Drop either of those and the cadence is still authentic but imperfect, which is why an analysis has to check the bass and the soprano separately rather than trusting an overall feeling of finality.
questions.hint: Check the progression, then the bass of the final chord, then the top voice of the final chord.

answer.exemplar: Three conditions have to hold together, and this cadence holds all three. First, the progression is dominant to tonic, which makes it authentic rather than plagal or deceptive; the G7 supplies the tritone that is obliged to resolve. Second, both chords are in root position, which the bass confirms by sounding the roots G2 and C3; without this the tonic chord could be an inversion and the ear would have to decide which note of it is the real goal. Third, the tonic is the highest voice, which the soprano confirms by rising from B4 to C5; this is the condition that makes the cadence perfect rather than merely authentic, because the ear follows the top line and the top line arrives on the tonic note. Each condition removes a different doubt: the first says a resolution has happened, the second says where the goal is, and the third says that the goal is in the position the listener is tracking. If the final chord were in first inversion, or the soprano ended on E or G, the cadence would still be authentic but imperfect. The wrong belief to avoid is that a cadence is perfect because it sounds conclusive, when the word names a checklist.

questions.learningObjective: state the spacing limit between adjacent upper voices in four-part writing
questions.explanation: The rule is that the soprano and the alto, and the alto and the tenor, must each lie within an octave of one another, so that the three upper voices sound as a single line. Here A3 to C5 spans 15 semitones, so the alto and the soprano break the rule, while C3 to F3 at 5 semitones and F3 to A3 at 4 are both comfortably within it. The reason the rule exists is perceptual rather than harmonic: a hole wider than an octave between the upper voices stops the soprano sounding like a continuation of the alto and splits the melody in two. The bass is deliberately exempt, because a wide gap at the bottom is idiomatic and does not break the sense of a line.
questions.hint: Measure each adjacent pair of voices and compare the figures with an octave of 12 semitones.

options.text: The alto and the soprano, since adjacent upper voices may not be more than an octave apart
The tenor and the bass, since the two lowest voices must always be an octave apart from each other
options.misconception: puts the limit on the lowest pair, which is the one the rule deliberately exempts

options.text: No pair, since the chord is in root position and root position is always well spaced
options.misconception: assumes root position guarantees spacing, which is a claim about harmony not distance

options.text: No pair, since a four-part chord may space its upper voices as widely as the music needs
options.misconception: denies the spacing limit exists, though the upper pair here is a tenth apart

questions.topic: Counting the pairs that break the spacing rule
questions.learningObjective: count the adjacent voice pairs in a chord that are more than an octave apart
questions.explanation: The three adjacent distances are 5 semitones from C3 up to F3, 4 semitones from F3 up to A3 and 15 semitones from A3 up to C5, so only the last pair breaks the limit of an octave and the answer is 1. The second route counts the pairs that comply: there are three adjacent pairs in a four-part texture and two of them measure 12 semitones or less, so 3 minus 2 is 1. The three figure is the trap, since it counts the pairs of voices rather than the pairs that are too wide, and the figure of 0 would come from testing the two lowest voices alone and forgetting the upper pair.
questions.hint: Measure all three adjacent gaps, then count only those above 12 semitones.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: How a secondary dominant tonicises
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes a chord a secondary dominant and what depends on its resolution
questions.explanation: Two things define a secondary dominant. Its root is a diatonic chord's dominant, a fifth above it, and it resolves to that chord; and it is a major triad, which in this key means its third has been raised, here from F to F sharp, so the chord carries its own leading tone to the note it is aimed at. The raised note is the audible evidence, because a listener hears a note a semitone below G and waits for G to arrive. The effect lasts only as long as the chord and its resolution, so the key itself is untouched: the passage can begin and end in C major while a single chord pulls temporarily towards G. Without the resolution the raised third is stranded, which is why an unresolved secondary dominant sounds like a mistake rather than like an open ending.
questions.hint: Ask which diatonic chord the new root is a fifth above, and what has happened to that chord's third.

answer.exemplar: A secondary dominant is a major triad whose root is a fifth above a diatonic chord and which then resolves to that chord, so it borrows the behaviour of the dominant and points it somewhere other than the tonic. Here D is a fifth above G, so the D major chord is the dominant of G, and it is written V of V in a key whose own dominant is G. What makes it sound like a dominant rather than an ordinary triad is its third: F sharp is a chromatic alteration of the diatonic F natural, and it stands a semitone below G, which is exactly the leading tone that forces the resolution. For as long as the chord sounds it tonicises G, so a passage can be in C major and yet be pulling towards G for the length of one chord. If it did not resolve, the F sharp would have nowhere to go: the raised note would be left without its goal, the expectation of arrival would be unfulfilled, and the passage would sound stranded rather than suspended. The wrong belief to avoid is that a secondary dominant changes the key outright, when it only borrows the dominant's pull for the moment.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The distance between the outer voices of a perfect cadence
questions.learningObjective: express the distance between two octaves-apart notes as a number of octaves
questions.explanation: C3 to C4 is one octave of 12 semitones and C4 to C5 is a second octave of 12, so the total is 24 semitones, which is 2 octaves. The second route divides instead of adding: the chromatic distance from C3 up to C5 is 24 semitones and an octave is 12, so 24 divided by 12 is 2. Both routes agree, and the figure matters because the distance between the outer voices is a quick check on a cadence: a wide outer interval is normal in four-part writing, whereas a close one can make the texture sound thin. The trap is 12, which is the distance in semitones rather than the number of octaves, and 1, which would place the soprano only an octave above the bass.
questions.hint: Count the semitones from the lower note to the higher one and divide by the size of an octave.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Classifying a cadence from its two chords and two voices
questions.learningObjective: rank four cadence classifications of one closing progression
questions.explanation: The progression is a dominant seventh to a root-position tonic with the tonic in the highest voice, and those three facts together are the definition of a perfect authentic cadence. The half cadence is the nearest error because it also involves the dominant, but a half cadence ends on the dominant, and here the phrase arrives on the tonic. The deceptive cadence is tempting because the leading tone does rise by a semitone, but a deceptive cadence is dominant to submediant, and here the tonic is actually supplied. The plagal reading confuses where a cadence ends with how it gets there, since a plagal cadence is subdominant to tonic and this is dominant to tonic.
questions.hint: Name the two chords first, then test the bass and the top voice of the final chord.

options.text: A perfect authentic cadence, since both chords are in root position and the tonic is in the top voice
A half cadence, since the phrase stops on the chord whose bass carries the unresolved pull
A deceptive cadence, since the leading tone rises a semitone and so the tonic is reached by step
A plagal cadence, since the final chord is the tonic and every cadence ending there is plagal

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Measuring a phrase in bars from its note values
questions.learningObjective: convert a list of note values into a number of bars in a stated metre
questions.explanation: A half note is worth 2 beats, so eight of them are 16 beats, and a bar of 4/4 holds 4 beats, so the line fills 16 divided by 4, which is 4 bars. The second route measures in bars rather than in beats: a half note occupies half of a 4/4 bar, so eight of them are 8 times one half, which is 4 bars. Both routes agree, and the figure is what makes the line an eight-note, four-bar phrase rather than an eight-bar one, which is a distinction a reader has to make explicitly because the number of notes and the number of bars are easy to confuse. The trap is 8, which is the number of notes rather than the number of bars.
questions.hint: Total the beats in the line, then divide by the number of beats in one bar of the metre.
